senses: to commit a fault, do something wrong; transgress, offend, err
la:verb:delinquo.html:
dē-linquo, līqui, lictum, 3 (
perf. delinquerunt, codd.), v. n. and a., to fail, be wanting.
Lit., to fail, be lacking, for the usual deficere (cf. 1. deliquium, = defectus—very rare): delinquere frumentum, Cael. ap. : delinquat aut superet aliquid tibi, Tubero ib.—
Trop. (class.), to fail, be wanting in one's duty; to commit a fault, to do wrong, transgress, offend; and, delinquere aliquid, to commit, do something wrong.
Absol.: QVOD POPVLVS HERMVNDVLVS HOMINESQVE POPVLI HERMVNDVLI ADVERSVS POPVLVM ROMANVM BELLVM FECERE DELIQVERVNTQVE, etc., an old formula used in declaring war,; cf. id. ap. : an quia non delinquunt viri?: ut condemnaretur filius aut nepos, si pater aut avus deliquisset?: mercede delinquere (opp. gratis recte facere), Dietsch: in vita,; cf.: in bello miles,; and: hac quoque in re,: in ancilla,: deliquere homines adulescentuli per ambitionem,: paulum deliquit amicus,: multo jam ut praestet laxitate delinquere,.—Of errors in language, .—
With acc. respect.: dum caveatur praeter aequum ne quid delinquat,; so, quid,; ; ; : quae,: quid erga aliquem,: quid ego tibi deliqui?.—With object. acc.: flagitia,; cf.: multo majora deliquit,.—Pass.: adulterium quod pubertate delinquitur,; cf. delictum.—Pass. impers.: ut nihil a me adhuc delictum putem,; .
la:verb:delinquo.inflection: līqui, lictum, 3, v. n. and a.

la:noun:delectatio.html:
dēlectātĭo, ōnis, f.
id.
,
a delighting, delight, pleasure, amusement (freq. and good prose): delectatio voluptas suavitate auditus animum deleniens, etc., : homo videndi et audiendi delectatione ducitur,; so, conviviorum,. More freq. without gen.: mira quaedam in cognoscendo suavitas et delectatio,; so, jucunditas delectatioque,; with voluptas,: (doctrina et literae), quae secundis rebus delectationem modo habere, videbantur, nunc vero etiam salutem,fin.: gratiam et delectationem afferunt,; et saep.; : in amicitia,.—In plural, —
As medic. t. t., a straining, effort, tenesmus (late Lat.): frequens ventris egerendi,; .

la:noun:deliberatio.html:
dēlībĕrātĭo, ōnis, f.
id.
,
a deliberation, consultation, consideration (a Ciceron. word; elsewhere very rare).
In gen.: ad deliberationes eas, quas habebat domi de republica, principes civitatis adhibebat,; : inciditur omnis jam deliberatio, si intellegitur non posse fieri,: id quod in deliberationem cadit,: habet res deliberationem,needs consideration,: consilii capiendi,respecting the resolution to be adopted,; cf. officii, et saep.: neque recte an perperam (factum) interpretor: fuerit ista ejus deliberatio, qui bellum suscepit,; . —
Esp. in rhetor. lang. i. q. causa deliberativa, ; ; .

la:verb:delibero.gloss: to weigh well, consider maturely, deliberate respecting a thing, ponder
senses: to weigh well, consider maturely, deliberate respecting a thing, ponder
to deliberate or consult, take counsel, advise upon (with an oracle)
la:verb:delibero.html:
dē-lībĕro, āvi, ātum, 1, v. a.
de and libro, libra; cf. Paul. ex Müll.: deliberare a libella, qua quid perpenditur dictum
,
to weigh well in one's mind, to consider maturely, deliberate respecting a thing; to take counsel, consult, advise upon (freq. and class.; for syn. cf. cogito, agito, volvo, reputo, perpendo, meditor, commentor, consulo).
Prop.
In gen.: re deliberata, post diem tertium ad Caesarem reversuros,; so, re deliberata,: delibera hoc, dum ego redeo,: de summa rerum deliberare,: de geographia etiam atque etiam,: de necanda filia,: de singulis articulis temporum,: deliberare Velitne an non,: utrum ... an (with concoquere),: an recipiat,; cf.: quando incipiendum sit,: ego amplius deliberandum censeo,; so absol., ; ; ; al.: cum aliquo de salute fortunisque alicujus,; ; cf.: cum judicibus quasi deliberamus,: cum cupiditate id est cum animi levissima parte deliberat,takes counsel of,: cum materia,: cum causis,: cum re praesenti,.—Pass. impers.: deliberatur de Avarico in communi concilio, incendi placeret an defendi,: ut utri potissimum consulendum sit deliberetur, —Prov.: deliberando saepe perit occasio, (Rib.): deliberandum est saepe, statuendum est semel,.—
In partic.
(Like consulo, no. I. B. 1.) To consult an oracle (only in Nepos): ex his delecti Delphos deliberatum missi sunt ... his consulentibus, etc.,: so with consulere,.—
Pass. impers.: deliberari, to be maturely discussed, hence to be in doubt, usually with potest, non potest, etc.: ex eo deliberari poterit, ducenda necne alvus sit,: neque maneatis aut abeatis deliberari potest,i. e. you must certainly go away,: M. Aemilius, qui pejor an ignavior sit, deliberari non potest,. Cf.: nemo deliberat, no one doubts, etc., . —
Meton. (causa pro effectu), to resolve, determine, after deliberation (rare in the verb. finit.; usually in the part. perf., with inf. or acc. and inf.): quod iste certe statuerat ac deliberaverat non adesse,: (Cleopatra) deliberata morte ferocior, * : certum ac deliberatum est me illis obsequi, Turpil. ap. , and 429, 21; so with certum,: cum mihi deliberatum et constitutum sit ita gerere consulatum, etc.,: sic habuisti statutum cum animo ac deliberatum, omnes judices reicere,: deliberatum est non tacere amplius, Afran. ap. Interpr. .—Hence, dēlībĕrātus, a, um, P. a., resolved upon, determined, certain (rare): neque illi quicquam deliberatius fuit quam me ... evertere,: instructius deliberatiusque,.

la:noun:delictum.html:
dēlictum, i, n.
delinquo
, prop. a falling

short of the standard of law (hence esp.

a transgression against positive law; cf. peccatum, usu. against natural law; cf. also: malefactum, maleficium, facinus, flagitium, scelus, nefas, impietas, culpa), a fault, offence, crime, transgression, wrong: delictum suom Suamque ut culpam expetere in mortalem sinat,; so, delictum in se admittere,: majore commisso delicto, * : quo delictum majus est, eo poena est tardior,: fatetur aliquis se peccasse et ejus delicti veniam petit: nefarium est facinus ignoscere. At leve delictum est; omnia peccata sunt paria,: ubi senatus delicti conscientia populum timet,; ; : defendere delictum,: praeoccupatus in delicto,: hostia pro delicto,a trespass-offering, et saep.—In plur., ; ; ; ; ; ; et saep.

la:noun:delicia.gloss: corner beam supporting a section of an outward-sloping roof
senses: corner beam supporting a section of an outward-sloping roof

la:noun:delicia#2.gloss: delight, pleasure (an activity which affords enjoyment)

la:noun:deliciae.gloss: delight, pleasure (an activity which affords enjoyment)
senses: delight, pleasure (an activity which affords enjoyment)
comforts, luxuries (conditions affording physical or mental ease)
la:noun:deliciae.html:
dēlĭcĭae, ārum, f. (sing.dēlĭcĭa, ae, f.;
ante-and post-class.,; ; ; : dēlĭcĭum, ii, n., ; ; ; ; ; ; sq.; 4394; 4958. And dēlĭcĭus, ii, m., Inscr. Don. cl. 1, 132, and ap. Gorium Columb. , no. 4) [delicio; that which allures, flatters the senses], delight, pleasure, charm, allurement; deliciousness, luxuriousness, voluptuousness, curiosities of art; sport, frolics, etc. (freq. and class.; for syn. cf.: voluptas, libido, delectatio, oblectatio, delectamentum, oblectamentum).
Prop.: cogitatio amoenitatum ad delectationem, aut supellectilis ad delicias, aut epularum ad voluptates,; cf. et saep.: deliciarum causa et voluptatis cives Romanos cum mitella saepe vidimus,: multarum deliciarum comes est extrema saltatio,: deliciis diffluentes,; ; ; et saep.: Herodotus Thucydidesque longissime a talibus deliciis vel potius ineptiis afuerunt,; cf. ; : delicias facere, to play tricks, to joke, to make sport of one, ; ; ; on the contrary, to sport as lovers, Catull. 45, 24; 72, 2: amores et hae deliciae quae vocantur,: votorum,a dallying with, fondly prolonging,: ecce aliae deliciae (pretensions) equitum vix ferendae, : esse in deliciis alicui,to be any one's favorite,; so ; : aliquid in deliciis habere,: habere aliquem in deliciis,: in deliciis vivere,. —
Transf., of living beings: delight, darling, sweetheart, beloved: tu urbanus scurra, deliciae popli,: mea voluptas, meae deliciae, mea vita, mea amoenitas,: amores ac deliciae tuae Roscius,; cf. ; ; and the well-known appellation of Titus: amor ac deliciae generis humani,: C. Sempronium Rufum mel ac delicias tuas, Cael. ap. : Corydon ardebat Alexim, Delicias domini,; cf. , : verba ne Alexandrinis quidem permittenda deliciis,favorite slaves,: aegrae solaque libidine fortes Deliciae,a voluptuary, minion,; ; ; cf. Plutarch, Anton. 59: delicias hominis,a precious fellow!.

senses: delegation of one person by another
la:noun:delegatio.html:
dēlēgātĭo, ōnis, f.
delego, no. II.
,
an assignment, substitution, delegation of one person by another.
Prop.: a mancipe,; of one thing for another: delegatione perfecta solutio,; cf. context.—
Trop.: necesse est ipse laborem impendas: delegationem res ista non recipit,.

la:verb:delecto.gloss: to delight, charm, please (+ accusative the person, who is delighted)
senses: to delight, charm, please (+ accusative the person, who is delighted)
la:verb:delecto.html:
dēlecto, āvi, ātum, 1,
v. intens. a. [delicio].
To allure from the right path, to entice away, to seduce (only ante-class.): me Apollo ipse delectat, ductat Delphicus, Enn. ap. (Trag. v. 390 Vahl.: delectare, illicere, attrahere, Non.): hostem, Quadrig. : ubi sementem facturus eris, ibi oves delectato,keep back, (also copied in ). —
Meton. (effectus pro causa), to delight, sc. by attracting, alluring; to please, charm, amuse (freq. and class.; cf.: oblecto, juvo): mentem atque animum delectat suum, Enn. ap. : Pamphilam arcesse, ut delectet hic nos,: non tam ista me sapientiae fama delectat, quam, etc.,; fin.: sive Falernum to magis delectat,—With abl.: delectari multis inanibus rebus, ut honore, ut gloria, etc.: animo autem virtute praedito ... non admodum delectari,: jumentis,: imperio,: criminibus inferendis,: carminibus,; cf. iambis (with gaudere carmine), et passim: interea cum Musis nos delectabimus aequo animo,; cf.: cum Musis delectari,.—With ab and abl.: ut me ab eo delectari facilius quam decipi putem posse,; so, ab aliquo,; et saep.—With in and abl.: in hoc admodum delector, quod, etc., Goer.; cf. ; ; cf.: ille me delectat in omni genere,: in alio sua quemque natura delectat,.—In ellipt. style, impers.: me magis de Dionysio delectat,—With inf. as subject: quam delectabat eum defectiones solis et lunae multo ante nobis praedicere,; ; : aedificare casas ... si quem delectet barbatum,; cf.: me pedibus delectat claudere verba,: delectat Veneris decerpere flores,.—In pass.: vir bonus et

prudens dici delector, ; : delectat, impers. (late Lat.), Boeth. Cons. Phil. 2, 3.

la:verb:delego.html:
dē-lēgo, āvi, ātum, 1,
v. a., to send, assign, dispatch, delegate a person to any place, person or business; to assign, confide, commit, intrust any thing to a person (for attention, care, protection, etc.); to charge a person with a business; to lay or impose upon a person any charge, order, business, command, etc., esp. of that which one prefers not to attend to in person (good prose; not in Caes.; perh. not in Cic.; v. the doubtful passage , and Orell. ad loc.).
In gen.
With personal objects: si cui fautores delegatos viderint, etc., and 83: aliquem in Tullianum,: infantem ancillis ac nutricibus,; cf. : Cassium Longinum occidendum delegaverat,: studiosos Catonis ad illud volumen delegamus,refer to,: ad senatum,fin.—
With a thing as object: hunc laborem alteri delegavi, Cael. ap. ; so, curam nepotum alicui,: officium alicui,: ministerium triumviris,; cf.: jurisdictionem magistratibus,: ordinandas bibliothecas alicui,; cf. : obsidione delegata in curam collegae,: delegato sibi officio functi sunt,. —
In partic., t. t. in the lang. of business, to assign, transfer, make over, either one who is to pay a debt or the debt itself: delegare est vice sua alium reum dare creditori, vel cui jusserit, : debitorem,: debitores nobis deos,; cf.: delegabo te ad Epicurum, ab illo fiet numeratio,: nomen paterni debitoris,.— Absol.: Quinto delegabo, si quid aeri meo alieno superabit,: Balbi regia condicio est delegandi,: terram,to assign,.—
Trop., to attribute, impute, ascribe to: si hoc crimen optimis nominibus delegare possumus,; so, causam peccati mortuis,: scelera ipsa aliis,: omne rei bene aut secus gestae in Etruria decus dedecusque ad Volumnium,; cf.: servati consulis decus ad servum,

la:verb:deligo.gloss: to pick off, pluck off; to cull
senses: to pick off, pluck off; to cull
la:verb:deligo.html:
dē-lĭgo, lēgi, lectum, 3, v. a.
1. lego
,
to choose out, to select (for syn. cf.: lego, coopto, designo, eligo, seligo).
In gen. (freq. and class.): continuo Amphitruo delegit viros primores principes,: ad eas res conficiendas Orgetorix deligitur,: quodsi liber populus deliget, quibus se committat; deligetque optimum quemque,: qui ex senatu in hoc consilium delecti estis,; so with ex, ; ; ; ; ; ; et saep.; poet. with ab: delectos ordine ab omni centum oratores,: Otho (Celsum) bello inter duces delegit,: locum castris,; : hunc sibi locum domicilio,fin. et saep.: re frumentaria comparata equitibusque delectis,; and so of soldiers,; ; : delecti Latio et Laurentibus agris,: melimela ad lunam delecta,.—Poet.: altaque mortali deligere astra manu, (3, 30, 50 M. dub.; al. deripere).—
In partic.
Of fruits, to gather, pick off: oleam,: uvam,: fructum,.—
With the accessory idea of removal to a distance, to choose out and send or take away (rare): amentem ex aedibus,: senes ac fessas aequore matres,.

la:verb:delabor.gloss: to fall, sink or slip down
senses: to fall, sink or slip down
la:verb:delabor.html:
dē-lābor, lapsus, 3,
v. dep. n., to fall, sink, slip down (freq. and class.).
Lit.: signum, de caelo delapsum,: de manibus audacissimorum civium delapsa arma,; : sinus ab humero,: ex utraque parte (aqua),: ex equo,: ab aethere, to glide down, poet. for to fly down, sc. to the earth, ; cf.: aetheriis ab astris,: caelo,: summo Olympo,: per auras,; also absol.: aquila leniter delapsa,: curru delapsus eodem,; cf. : serta capiti delapsa,: in terram delabi,: in scrobes,: de caelo in provinciam,, 1, 2: in mare (flumen),: sensit medios delapsus in hostes,: te aequoream Lemnon,: voce delapsa a magnifica gloria, .—
Trop. (esp. freq. in Cic.), to come down, sink, descend; and with reference to the term. ad quem, to slide or fall into: jam a sapientium familiaritatibus ad vulgares amicitias oratio nostra delabitur,; cf. ; ; and: aut a minoribus ad majora ascendimus, aut a majoribus ad minora delabimur,: in idem genus morbi delapsa,; cf.: in hoc vitium scurrile,: in amorem libertae,: in ambitionem, et saep.: cujus in similitudinem proclivi cursu delabitur,: in istum sermonem,: in eas difficultates, ut, etc.,; cf.: eo, ut, etc.,: ad aequitatem et ad rerum naturam,: ad impatientiam,: ad inopiam,fin.—Of sounds, to descend, be derived: atque etiam illa sunt ab his delapsa plura genera (vocum),.—In epistolary style: eo magis delabor ad Clodiam, I incline to Clodia (i. e. to purchase her gardens), .

senses: to finish, terminate, put an end to
to delete (e.g. Ecclesiastical: from the book of life)
la:verb:deleo.html:
dēlĕo, lēvi, lētum, 2 (
perf. sync. delerunt, : delerit,; : delerat,: delerant,; plqpf. subj. sync. delesset, ; ; part. perf. dēlĭtus: litterae delitae, Varr. ap. : epistola delita, Calvus ib.; Cic. Ep. ap. ; cf. 1. aboleo), v. a.
Sanscr. R. lī, adhere; cf.: vi-lī, dissolve; Gr. λίμνη, λιμήν, λειμών, etc.; Lat. lino, perf. levi; polio, etc.; cf. also Gr. λιμός, Lat. lētum
, to abolish, destroy, annihilate (freq. and class.; cf.: eluo, diluo, diruo, exstinguo, everto, demolior, destruo).
Of objects not personal: si certo tempore luna Gignitur et certo deletur tempore rursus, (for which, shortly before, nova luna creari ... aborisci): si Juppiter saepe urbes delevit, fruges perdidit, etc.,; so, urbem Numantiam, Carthaginem, etc.,, 12 fin.; ; ; ; ; cf.: magnam Graeciam,: nomen Aequorum prope ad internecionem,; and, Volscum nomen,: sepulcrum,: aedificia, al.: epistulas,; so of the blotting out, effacing, obliterating, of writing, ; ; ; ; ; ; ; : stigmata in facie,: radices, —
Trop., to finish, stop, terminate, end: praesentia, futura bella,: omnes leges una rogatione,: omnia morte, id. Lael, 4, 13: omnem memoriam discordiarum oblivione sempiterna,; cf. : nec si quid olim lusit Anacreon, Delevit aetas,; trop.: deleo omnes dehinc ex animo mulieres (i. e. memoriam mulierum),: veritatem (simulatio),: omnem molestiam,: improbitatem (with exstinguere),; cf.: turpitudinem fugae virtute,: priorem ignominiam,.—
Of personal objects: dispersis ac paene deletis hostibus,destroyed, annihilated,; so milit.,; ; ; ; ; ; : homines morte deletos,: toto animante deleto,; rarely of a single person: C. Curionem,

la:verb:delibo.gloss: to take off or away (a little)
senses: to take off or away (a little)
la:verb:delibo.html:
dē-lībo, āvi, ātum, 1,
v. a., to take off, take away a little from any thing; of food, to taste (class.).
Lit.: parvam delibet ab aequore partem,: aliquid membrorum,: truncum,: paululum carnis,; cf. cenas (opp. edere), Favor. ap. —
Trop.
To take, enjoy, pluck, gather: flos delibatus populi Suadaeque medulla, the picked flower of the people, Enn. ap. : ut omni ex genere orationem aucuper et omnes undique flosculos carpam atque delibem,cull,: ex universa mente divina delibatos animos habere,: novum honorem,to taste, enjoy,; cf.: honores parcissime,: oscula, ; : artes,: omnia narratione,to touch upon,; cf. ; : delibor, I am ripe for plucking, i. e. about to die, . —
To take away, detract from, diminish: neque úlla Res animi pacem delibat,: de laude jejuni hominis delibare quicquam,: aliquid de honestate,: de gloria sua,: de virginitatis integritate,; cf.: castitatem virginis,ext.: pudicitiam,: nec vitam ducendo demimus hilum Tempore de mortis nec delibare valemus,—Poet., transf.: Delibata deum per te tibi numina sancta Saepe oberunt,disparaged,; cf.: ille (Gracchus) nulla voce delibans insitam virtutem concidit tacitus,.

la:verb:delitisco.gloss: to hide, or go into hiding

la:verb:delitesco.gloss: to hide, or go into hiding
senses: to hide, or go into hiding
la:verb:delitesco.html:
dē-lĭtesco, tŭi, 3,
v. inch. n. [latesco], to hide away, conceal one's self; to lie hid, to lurk (class.).
Lit.: bestiae in cubilibus delitescunt,; cf.: hostes noctu in silvis delituerant, * : caelum,: in ulva,: sub praesepibus vipera,: silvā,; cf.: privato loco,: sinu ancillae,: ut eo mitteret amicos, qui delitescerent, deinde repente prosilirent,fin.—Absol.: delituit mala,.—
Transf., of things: stella cursum conflcit, vespertinis temporibus delitescendo,.—Of a letter: ancillae sinu,.—
Trop., to skulk behind, shelter one's self under: in alicujus auctoritate delitesceret,; so, in ista calumnia,; cf. : in dolo malo, id. Tull. § 33: umbrā magni nominis,; Zumpt N. cr.

la:noun:delubrum.html:
dēlūbrum, i, n.
de-luo, the place of expiation
,
a temple, shrine, sanctuary (class., esp. freq. in poets and in elevated prose; usually in the plur.; for syn. cf.: templum, aedes, fanum, cella, sacellum, sacrarium).
Plur.: CONSTRVCTA A PATRIBVS DELVBRA IN VRBIBVS HABENTO, etc.,: est mihi tecum pro aris et focis certamen et pro deorum templis atque delubris,; cf. coupled with fana, id. Rab. perd. 10 fin.: ante deum delubra,; ; ; ; ; ; ; et saep.; : ; ; ; ; : idolorum,—
Sing.: noctu audita ex delubro vox est, etc.,: so coupled with templa,: Smyrnaei delubrum ejus (sc. Homeri) in oppido dedicaverunt,; so Quirini,: ex alto delubri culmine,: Martis,.

la:noun:Delos.html:
Dēlos, i, f., Δῆλος,
a small island in the Aegean Sea, one of the Cyclades, the birthplace of Apollo and Diana, now Dili, Mela, 2, 7, 11; ; ; ; ; ; ; ; ; et saep.—Acc.: Delum, and 18 (repeatedly); : Delon, ; ; Mela, 3, 5, 2 al. —

Dēlĭus, a, um, adj., of Delos, Delian: tellus,i. e. Delos,: Apollo,; ; ; the same also vates,; and absol.: Delius, ; ; ; ; ; cf. also, folia,i. e. of the laurel,: antra,i. e. the oracle,: furta,i. e. the secret loves of Apollo,; Delia dea,i. e. Diana,; also absol.: Dēlĭa, = Diana, ; ; ; —

Transf., soft, tender, delicate (poet. and in post-Aug. prose): capella,; cf.: puella tenellulo delicatior haedo,: oves,: Anio delicatissimus amnium,; cf.: ad aquam,: delicatior teneriorque cauliculus,; .—
Addicted to pleasure; luxurious, voluptuous; and subst., a voluptuary, a wanton.
Prop.: adolescens,: pueri,: juventus,; cf.: odia libidinosae et delicatae juventutis, et saep.: quosdam e gratissimis delicatorum, i. e. of the paramours, παιδικῶν, ; cf. in the fem.: Flavia Domitilla, Statilii Capellae delicata,; et luxuriosus,; in inscriptions, delicatus and delicata simply mean favorite slave (cf. our terms valet and chamber-maid), -2805 and 4650.—
Transf.
Spoiled with indulgence, delicate, dainty, effeminate: nimium ego te habui delicatam (I have spoiled you), : equorum cursum delicati minutis passibus frangunt,; .—
Fastidious, scrupulous: aures,; vah delicatus!.—Hence, adv.: dēlĭcātē.
